messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At fifty-one, Dr. Lien Nguyen had built a quiet, orderly life around her dental practice in a suburban strip mall. That order had been shattered four years earlier, when a former patient began a campaign of stalking that lasted eighteen months. He had sent letters to her office, left voicemails at the reception desk, and once, just once, she had heard a song playing from his car stereo as he sat in the parking lot — a melancholic ballad she had hummed while adjusting his crown, and which he must have recorded. The memory of that song, drifting through the closed blinds of her operator room, still made her stomach drop. She called the police, who took a report but could not arrest him until he violated a restraining order. By then the damage was done: Lien had learned that safety was something other people promised but could not deliver.

Months passed, and she returned to work. But the world had grown porous. When a patient’s phone rang with a familiar melody — the same minor-key progression, the same lazy guitar — she felt the threat before she could name it. Her chest would tighten, her gaze would sweep the waiting room for exits, and she would excuse herself to the sterilization alcove, where she pressed her back against the wall until the feeling passed. Even when her husband assured her the stalker was in another state, that the police had confirmed it, Lien found the words meaningless. “I know you’re safe,” he would say, and she would nod, but inside she knew safety was not a thing you could know, only a thing you could fail to lose. She began to choose her seat carefully everywhere she went: always a table with a wall behind her, never a booth in the center of the room. At the office she rearranged her own treatment station so that her dental chair faced the door and her back rested against a solid partition. It was the only way she could concentrate on a root canal without her neck prickling.

Then a true-crime podcast about stalking appeared in her recommended feed. She did not click, but the thumbnail — a shadowy figure behind a chain-link fence — stayed with her for days. Related media exposure, she later learned to call it, but at the time it simply felt like a door swinging open. After that, she found herself scanning news headlines for similar stories, as if preparing for an ambush. The sight of a police cruiser in her neighborhood no longer brought relief; it brought a flash of that afternoon when an officer had told her, with kind eyes, that they could not watch her house every night. Police presence now meant the threat was real, not that it was handled. She would drive an extra block to avoid passing the precinct.

The cycle tightened. A song on the office radio meant she could not focus; she would ask the hygienist to change the station, and then feel ashamed. A news article about stalking meant she would lie awake, replaying the old voicemails in her mind. Each trigger fed the same conviction: the world was not safe, and her own vigilance was the only barrier between her and catastrophe. She stopped attending her weekly mahjong group because the host’s house did not have a single seat that faced both the door and a window. The consequences were concrete: friendships frayed, and her husband quietly stopped suggesting date nights because she would scan the restaurant for exits rather than look at him.

What finally brought Lien to seek help was not a crisis but a quiet exhaustion. She had just finished a crown preparation, and a pop song from the common playlist had made her hands shake so badly she had to pause. As she dismissed the patient, she realized she could no longer distinguish between reasonable caution and a life ruled by fear. She wanted to believe that safety could be learned, not merely defended. She was not sure it was possible, but she was willing to sit down with a stranger and try.
